subject: Computer Networking
title: Passwords and Their Problems
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Passwords and Their Problems.

hook.text: The most common password is still '123456.' Billions of accounts are protected by guesses a child could make.

buildup.text: Passwords are hashed before storage. But weak passwords produce hashes that attackers can crack in seconds.

discovery.text: Salting adds random data before hashing. Identical passwords produce different hashes, blocking rainbow tables.

twist.text: Password reuse is the real epidemic. One breached site gives attackers credentials they try everywhere else.

climax.text: Password managers generate and store unique passwords for every site. They're the best defense against reuse.

punchline.text: A strong, unique password per site. That's the minimum.

quiz.question: Why is password reuse dangerous?
options: One breach gives attackers credentials to try on other sites
It makes passwords easier to remember
It slows down the login process

details.summary: Passwords remain the most common authentication method despite their many weaknesses. Users reuse passwords across sites, choose predictable ones, and fall for phishing. Password attacks include brute force, dictionary attacks, credential stuffing, and rainbow table lookups against stolen hashes.
details.whyItMatters: Weak and reused passwords are the root cause of most account compromises. Understanding password vulnerabilities explains why additional authentication factors are necessary.
takeaways: Password reuse makes one breach compromise many accounts
Credential stuffing tests stolen passwords across multiple sites
Password managers generate and store unique strong passwords

faq.question: Why are passwords considered insecure?
faq.answer: Humans create predictable passwords, reuse them across sites, and fall for phishing that steals them. Billions of stolen credentials are available from past breaches. Even strong passwords can be captured through keyloggers, phishing, or server-side breaches.

faq.question: What makes a strong password?
faq.answer: Length is more important than complexity. A 20-character passphrase like four random words is stronger than a short complex password. Never reuse passwords across sites. Use a password manager to generate and store unique passwords.
